open-question.question: Beyond refusing an empty title or body, does the task-list tool validate an authored section against task-format.md (title of 4 to 8 title-cased words, a 1 to 3 sentence body, no sub-heading or labeled section inside the body), or does it accept any body text as the section's prose and leave the format to the authoring skills?
open-question.alternative: The insert and append subcommands refuse, with one Error: line and the files unchanged, only a title or body that would break the tool's own parse: a title holding a line break, and a body holding a line that the parser reads as a section boundary (a bare `---` line or a line opening with `## `). Everything else — heading lines at other levels, labeled sections, title length and case, sentence count — is accepted as prose and left to the authoring skills; the move copies its section as it stands. Guarantees that every section the tool writes is parsed back as exactly that section, which is the property a sole writer exists to secure, while keeping the tool free of any authoring rule, so task-format.md stays the only home of the format and no brief is refused for its wording. The ban on sub-headings and labeled sections, the property task altitude protects most directly, stays prose-only, so a `**Steps:**` block or a `### Notes` heading inside a body is still written without complaint.

Beyond refusing an empty title or body, the insert and append subcommands write whatever title and body they are given verbatim, including a body line that reads as a `---` separator or a `## ` heading; the move copies its section as it stands. Every rule in task-format.md, structural or quantitative, stays with the authoring skills exactly as today, and the tool checks none of it. The smallest tool and the simplest contract: the tool is a pure writer with no format knowledge, task-format.md stays the single home of the format, and no authored brief is ever refused for its wording, so a headless derive or submit run never stops on a format judgment. The tool can write a file its own parser then splits differently (a body holding a `---` line becomes two sections and the next move slices it wrongly), so the sole writer does not guarantee the shape it parses; and the format rules stay unenforced, as they are today.

The insert and append subcommands refuse the parse-breaking title or body of the integrity guard and, in addition, any body line that opens a sub-heading (a line opening with `#` at any level) or a labeled section (a line that is a bold label ending in a colon, such as `**Steps:**`, `**Notes:**`, or `**Verified:**`). Title length, title case, and sentence count are not checked and stay with the authoring skills; the move copies its section as it stands. Enforces mechanically, with deterministic line-level tests that need no heuristic, the one rule whose breach changes a task's altitude (no steps, notes, success, or Verified section in an authored brief), and keeps a `**Verified:**` label out of TASKS_TODO.md where it would confuse the completion bar. Puts a second statement of part of the format in the tool, so a later change to task-format.md's structural rule must be mirrored in code and tests; and a body that legitimately quotes a bold-labelled phrase on its own line is refused.

The insert and append subcommands refuse everything the structural checks refuse and, in addition, a title whose whitespace-split word count falls outside 4 to 8. Title case and the 1 to 3 sentence count are not checked, because neither has an unambiguous mechanical test, and stay with the authoring skills; the move copies its section as it stands. Enforces every rule of task-format.md that has a deterministic test and no other, so the tool never refuses on a heuristic misjudgment, while a title too short to be unique or too long to be a handle is stopped at write time. The numeric title bound now lives in task-format.md and in the tool and must be kept in step by hand; and the body length, the rule most often stretched in practice, stays unenforced.

The insert and append subcommands refuse every rule of task-format.md they can test: the parse-breaking and structural lines above, a title outside 4 to 8 words, a title that is not title-cased by a fixed rule the tool defines (for example every word opening with a capital or a non-letter), and a body whose counted sentences fall outside 1 to 3 by a fixed counting rule the tool defines (for example sentence-ending punctuation followed by whitespace or the end of the body, outside code spans). There is no override; the move copies its section as it stands. The tool becomes the complete enforcement point of the task format, so no runner, headless or not, can write a brief that drifts from the template, and the format rules gain the tests the authoring prose never had. The sentence count and title-case tests are heuristics (abbreviations such as `e.g.`, file names, decimals, and minor words in titles all misfire), so legitimate briefs are refused and a headless derive or submit run stops on a false positive; one milestone-41 brief already holds four sentences by a naive count, and the format's numbers gain a second home in the tool.

The insert and append subcommands run the full set of checks of the full format refusal by default, but accept a flag (for example `--allow-format`) under which the length, case, and sentence-count checks are skipped while the parse-breaking and structural checks still apply; the authoring skills pass the flag only after re-reading a refused brief and judging the breach deliberate. The move copies its section as it stands. Keeps the full format enforced by default while giving a runner a deliberate way past a heuristic false positive, so a legitimate four-sentence brief is written rather than mangled to satisfy a counter. Adds a flag and a refusal-then-retry turn to the authoring skills' prose, and a flag a runner may pass reflexively erodes the check it exists to soften; the format's numbers still gain a second home in the tool.

The insert and append subcommands enforce only the parse-integrity guard and otherwise write the section as given; the tool gains a separate read-only subcommand (for example `check`) that reports, one line per finding in the read contract's bare-value style, every section of a task file breaching a structural, title-length, title-case, or sentence-count rule of task-format.md, which an authoring skill may run after writing and a reviewer may run at any time. Nothing is refused for format. Gives the format a mechanical check, heuristics included, without ever blocking a write on a false positive, and keeps every mutator's "prints nothing on success" contract intact. A check nobody is required to act on can be skipped or ignored, so the format is no more enforced than today unless the authoring prose adds a step to run it and react, which costs a tool call and turn per run; and it adds a subcommand and a second home for the format's numbers.

The insert and append subcommands enforce only the parse-integrity guard as a refusal, and for every structural, title-length, title-case, or sentence-count breach of task-format.md still write the section but print one warning line per breach on stderr and exit 0. Nothing is refused for format; the move copies its section as it stands. The runner sees each format breach in the very call that wrote the section, with no extra subcommand or turn, and no heuristic misfire ever blocks a write. Breaks the shared tool contract that a mutator prints nothing on success, so callers and tests can no longer read any stderr output as failure, and a warning arriving after the write leaves the runner either to ignore it or to spend a further call correcting a section already on disk.

open-question.question: Does the task-list tool parse a whole task file and re-render it in one canonical layout on every write, normalizing the blank-line convention of every section it did not touch, or does it splice only the bytes of the section it adds or removes and leave every other byte of the file as it stands?
open-question.alternative: On every write (initialize, append, insert, move) the tool parses the whole task file into its heading line and its ## sections (title, body prose, and for a done entry the **Verified:** bullets), applies the change to that model, and renders the entire file in one canonical layout: a blank line after the heading, after the body, after the label, after the last bullet, after each ---, and the file ending in --- plus one newline. Every section the call did not touch is re-emitted in that layout too, so any blank-line drift in it is normalized silently on the first write; the body prose itself is carried through as parsed text. The file is replaced through the same-directory temporary file, as open_questions.py does. One write path that mirrors open_questions.py's render-then-replace, so output is deterministic and testable against golden fixtures, and the seam failures runners hit today (a milestone-45 agent ran a second script to restore the blank line between a --- and the next heading) cannot occur anywhere in the file, which converges on the documented convention after one write. The first write to a file that drifted (milestone_41 ends in an extra blank line, milestone_42 holds a double blank, milestone_30 lacks a blank after a separator) or that someone edited by hand rewrites sections the commit is not about, so the Task-completion or Task-submission diff carries unrelated whitespace churn; and the parser must round-trip every body shape (internal paragraph breaks, lists, fenced code with blank lines) or it alters content it was never asked to touch. How strict that parse is depends on the unterminated-section and format-validation axes the sibling questions own.

The tool parses and renders the whole file in the one canonical layout, as above, but before writing it re-renders the file as read and compares it to the bytes on disk: if the two differ, the call is refused with one Error: line naming the file and the files are left unchanged; only a file already in canonical form is written, through the same render-then-replace path. Initialization, which replaces the contents by design, is the one write not gated on the old bytes. Keeps the single deterministic render path and its testability while guaranteeing the tool never silently changes a byte of a section it was not asked to touch, so every task commit's diff is exactly the change made, and drift is surfaced the moment it appears instead of being absorbed. Any hand edit or historical drift that is not byte-canonical blocks every subsequent tool call on that file until someone fixes it by hand, which stops a headless complete-all-tasks run mid-milestone on a cosmetic difference; and body text the parser cannot round-trip exactly becomes a refusal rather than a write, so the parser's fidelity is load-bearing for availability.

The tool parses only to locate boundaries (the target section's ## line through its ---, or the anchor's position) and writes by splicing: a removal deletes exactly that byte span, an insertion or append places a canonically rendered new section at the located offset, and every other byte of the file, including the whitespace around the splice point, stays as it stands. No section, separator, or blank line outside the inserted or removed span is rewritten; the file is still replaced atomically through a same-directory temporary file. The tool changes nothing it was not asked to change, so diffs are minimal, hand-edited or drifted sections survive untouched, and the parser need only find headings and separators rather than model and round-trip every body shape. The new section inherits whatever whitespace its neighbour leaves, so a neighbour missing its trailing blank line yields a heading jammed against a --- (the exact repair a milestone-45 agent had to script), and removing a section can leave a double blank or none; layout consistency is not guaranteed, drift accumulates, and tests must cover splice offsets rather than one rendered form. Locating boundaries still depends on how the unterminated-section sibling resolves a section with no ---.

The tool keeps every byte of every untouched section exactly as it stands, as in a pure splice, but normalizes the whitespace at each junction its own write creates: an inserted or appended section gets exactly one blank line before its ## heading and one after its ---, and the gap a removed section leaves collapses to the single blank line the convention calls for, with the end of file normalized to --- plus one newline only when the write touched the end. Drift anywhere away from a junction is left in place. Combines a minimal diff and no silent rewriting of other sections with a guarantee that every seam the tool produces is well-formed, so the jammed-heading and doubled-blank failures cannot be introduced by a write even into a drifted file. It is a third behaviour with its own rules to specify and test (which whitespace counts as part of a seam, what happens at the file heading and at end of file), more logic than either a render or a raw splice, and it still leaves the file internally inconsistent wherever drift sits away from a junction, so the file never converges on the convention by itself.

open-question.question: How does submit-task tell the task-list tool where its one authored section goes: through a single insert subcommand whose position is an optional flag naming the anchor heading (before or after it, defaulting to the end of the file when no flag is given), or through separate subcommands for the append position and the anchored positions?
open-question.alternative: One `insert` subcommand carries every position submit-task can choose. The anchor is given by one of two mutually exclusive flags, `--before <Task Title>` or `--after <Task Title>`. When neither flag is given, the section goes at the end of `TASKS_TODO.md`. No separate append subcommand exists for submit-task. Submit-task's step 5 shows one fixed command whose only variation is an optional flag, so the three positions of step 3 map onto one code path and one test file. It also follows the open-question tool's habit of one subcommand per concern with modifier flags (`strip --recommendation`, `list --without-alternatives`), and argparse's mutually exclusive group rejects `--before` and `--after` together for free. The end-of-file position is implicit, so a runner that meant to anchor the section but dropped the flag still gets a successful insert at the end, the one silent misplacement left now that an unknown anchor is refused. Because no append subcommand stands beside it, the goal's wording of append as a distinct operation is carried by `insert` without a flag.

One `insert` subcommand whose position is required and always explicit: exactly one of `--end`, `--before <Task Title>`, or `--after <Task Title>`, held in a required mutually exclusive group. A call with no position flag is a malformed invocation and gets argparse's exit 2. There is no default position and no separate append subcommand. Every call states where the section goes, so the three choices submit-task's step 3 makes all show on the command line, and a forgotten anchor fails loudly instead of landing at the end. This matches the milestone's decision to refuse an unknown anchor rather than fall back to appending. The commonest case, appending, needs a flag that carries no information beyond "nothing else was chosen". The required-group form is also a usage shape neither existing tool has, so its exit-2 behaviour needs its own tests alongside the contract tests.

One `insert` subcommand takes one `--position` value written in submit-task's own vocabulary verbatim (`append`, `before: <Task Title>`, or `after: <Task Title>`). The tool parses the keyword prefix and the title after it, and refuses any other form with one `Error:` line. Whether the value is optional, defaulting to `append`, or required is part of the same contract and is fixed when the option is specified. The position submit-task decides in step 3 passes to the tool exactly as written, so the skill's prose and the command share one vocabulary and the runner does not translate a decision into flags. The tool has to own a small grammar of its own (prefix keywords, the colon, surrounding whitespace, a title that itself contains `: `) that argparse would otherwise check. That parsing means more code and more refusal tests, and quoting a title inside the value is fragile in a shell call. How fragile depends on how the sibling insert-input-shape question places the task title itself on the command line.

Two subcommands. `append` adds the one authored section at the end of `TASKS_TODO.md` and takes no position. `insert` takes a required anchor through one of the mutually exclusive flags `--before <Task Title>` or `--after <Task Title>`, and is refused by argparse without one. Submit-task's step 5 shows both commands and uses the one its step 3 decision names. It follows the goal's own wording, which names "inserts a positioned section" and "appends" as separate operations, and the open-question tool's precedent of an `add` that only appends. Each subcommand has one fixed shape with no default to reason about, and a missing anchor on `insert` is a usage error rather than a silent append. One skill needs two writing subcommands and two command shapes in its prose, and their duplicate-title check, input reading, and separator handling are duplicated or factored behind them. The recorded decision on derive-tasks already leaves append with a one-section form "only for submit-task's use, if any", so this option keeps a subcommand whose only caller is a branch of one skill.

Three subcommands, `append`, `insert-before`, and `insert-after`. The two anchored ones take the anchor title as a required positional argument after `MILESTONE_DIR`, and none of the three takes a position flag. Each position submit-task's step 3 can choose is its own fixed command. Every command is fully fixed in shape with no flags, defaults, or mutually exclusive groups, so argparse alone checks the arity and the subcommand name in the runner's prose spells out the decision. The tool surface triples for a single caller, with three near-identical subcommands, three sets of contract tests, and three commands in submit-task's step 5. Taking the anchor as a positional argument also competes for position with the task title if the sibling insert-input-shape question puts the title on the command line, so two bare titles would sit side by side and be easy to swap.

open-question.question: When the task-list tool writes one authored section for submit-task, does it take the task title as a command-line argument and only the body prose on standard input (the open-question tool's add form), or does it read the whole section on standard input in the task file's own ## heading, body, and --- form, the same shape the initialize subcommand reads for derive-tasks?
open-question.alternative: The insert subcommand takes the task title as a positional command-line argument after MILESTONE_DIR and reads only the body prose on standard input as a quoted heredoc, the open-question tool's add form. The tool composes the ## heading line, the body, and the trailing --- itself. A ## line, a --- line, or any heading text in the piped body is not treated as structure. The initialize subcommand keeps reading whole sections on standard input, so the tool has two input shapes: argument plus body for the one-section insert, section form for the list. The runner cannot malform the section's structure, because the tool writes the heading and the separator itself. The title is a visible, separately checked argument (an empty title is refused on its own), the same shape as the anchor it may name. It follows the open_questions.py add precedent that every runtime site already uses: an id on argv, free text on stdin. The tool carries two input contracts and two validation paths for what is one section shape in the file, so insert and initialize can drift on what counts as a valid title or body. submit-task authors its section from task-format.md's template, which shows the heading and the ---, and must then split that section into an argument and a heredoc, quoting the title for the shell. How much the tool checks the title and body beyond emptiness is owned by the format-validation sibling.

The insert subcommand takes no title argument and reads one whole section on standard input in the task file's own form: the ## heading, the body, and the --- separator. It uses the same parser initialize uses for derive-tasks' list, but requires exactly one section and refuses with one Error: line and the file unchanged when stdin holds no section, holds text before the heading, or holds a second ## heading. One input shape and one parser serve every write of an authored section, so insert and initialize validate titles, bodies, and separators identically by construction. submit-task pipes exactly the section it authored from task-format.md's template, unchanged, the same shape derive-tasks pipes. The exactly-one rule turns a stray ## line in a body into a refusal instead of a silently split task. It departs from the open-question tool's argv-id, stdin-body precedent. The title is no longer a visible argument beside the anchor; it is found only by parsing the heredoc. The tool must define and test refusals for malformed piped structure (missing heading, leading text, a missing or extra ---) that the argument form never meets. How deeply the parsed section is checked against task-format.md is owned by the format-validation sibling.

The insert subcommand takes no title argument and reads one or more whole sections on standard input in the task file's ## heading, body, and --- form, through initialize's own parser with no count rule. Every section lands contiguously, in the piped order, at the one position the call names, all in one atomic write that is refused whole if any section is refused. submit-task pipes a list of one. Insert and initialize share not just a parser but an identical input contract, differing only in whether the file is replaced or added to. A future caller, such as discuss-new-task's ordered multi-task handoff, could then land several dependent sections at one position in one write and one commit instead of one submit-task run per piece. No current caller needs more than one section: submit-task authors exactly one, and discuss-new-task hands off by invoking submit-task once per task. The wider contract adds behaviour, and tests for it, that nothing exercises. It also lets an accidental ## line in a body become a second task that is inserted silently rather than refused. Commit subjects stay per-task (Task-submission: <task title>), which a multi-section insert does not fit.

open-question.question: Does the task-list tool require the fixed first-line heading of each task file it writes to (# TASKS TODO or # TASKS DONE), refusing with one Error: line a file whose first line is anything else, or does it treat whatever stands before the first ## section as opaque content that it carries through unchanged and never checks?
open-question.alternative: Before any insert, append, or move, the tool checks that the first line of each task file it is about to write is exactly its fixed heading (# TASKS TODO for TASKS_TODO.md, # TASKS DONE for TASKS_DONE.md). Any other first line, an empty file included, is refused with one Error: line naming the file, and both files stay byte-for-byte unchanged. Anything else standing between that heading and the first ## section is carried through unchanged and never checked. Initialize keeps its recorded behaviour of replacing TASKS_TODO.md whole, writing the heading itself, so it does not check the old first line. It catches a file that is not a task file at all, such as a truncated, overwritten, or hand-mangled one, before the tool splices sections into it. It costs nothing today, since all 92 task files in the repository's 46 milestone directories start with exactly the heading define_milestone.py writes, and it still leaves any note a person adds under the heading alone. The tool picks both paths itself from MILESTONE_DIR, so a swapped or wrong file can only come from a hand edit, and the check mostly guards a case that never occurs. It also makes a cosmetic edit to the heading line, like a changed case or a trailing word, a hard stop for every completion, submission, and append until someone repairs the line by hand. It adds one more refusal path that needs its own tests.

The tool checks the whole preamble, not just its first line, before any insert, append, or move. Everything before the first ## section must be exactly the fixed heading for that file followed by nothing but blank lines. A different first line, an empty file, or any other text in the preamble is refused with one Error: line and both files left byte-for-byte unchanged. Initialize keeps replacing TASKS_TODO.md whole and checks nothing. The files keep exactly the shape define_milestone.py creates and the task format describes, so no text outside a ## section can slip in unnoticed. The tool's own parser never has to decide what non-section text before the first heading means. A note a person adds under the heading, which is harmless to every reader of the files, blocks every write to that file until it is removed by hand. That makes it the strictest option and the one most likely to stop a headless completion chain over a cosmetic detail. The preamble is also checked by a rule that nothing else in the workflow states or needs.

The tool never checks the heading. Whatever stands before the first ## section in a task file, whether the fixed heading, other text, or nothing at all, is treated as opaque content and carried through byte-for-byte on every insert, append, and move. Initialize keeps its recorded behaviour of replacing TASKS_TODO.md whole with the fixed heading followed by the list. It adds no refusal path and no rule beyond the ## and --- sections the tool actually works on. A hand edit above the first section never blocks a completion or a submission, and the tool's job stays limited to the sections it moves and inserts, which is all the decisions recorded so far define. A task file whose top has been damaged or replaced is written into without complaint, so the corruption carries forward silently until a person or a reading skill notices it. The fixed heading becomes a convention that only define_milestone.py and initialize enforce, and the first-line contract nothing else checks drifts with every hand edit.

The tool never refuses over the preamble and never checks it. On every write to a task file it discards whatever stands before the first ## section and writes the fixed heading for that file plus one blank line in its place, so every file the tool has touched starts with the canonical preamble. Initialize does the same for TASKS_TODO.md as part of its whole-file replacement. The files heal themselves: a damaged, missing, or altered heading is corrected on the next write and never blocks a run, and the task files converge on the shape define_milestone.py creates without anyone having to repair them by hand. Any text a person put above the first section is silently dropped on the next completion or submission, with nothing printed, and only the commit diff shows it, which is the silent loss the tool's contract otherwise avoids. Whether rewriting bytes outside the section being written fits depends on the whole-file-rewrite-or-splice axis owned by a sibling question.

The tool never refuses over the preamble. On every write to a task file it makes sure the first line is the fixed heading for that file. If the first line is a single-# heading with different text, the tool replaces it with the fixed heading. If the file starts with anything else, such as a ## section, plain text, or nothing, the tool inserts the fixed heading and a blank line above it. Any other preamble text is carried through unchanged. A missing or altered heading is repaired without ever blocking a run, and unlike rewriting the whole preamble it keeps any note a person added under the heading. It needs a repair rule (replace or insert) that is more complex than either checking the heading or ignoring it, and that rule has to be tested. It still rewrites a line outside the section being written without saying so, which depends on the whole-file-rewrite-or-splice axis owned by a sibling question. A file that is not a task file at all gets a heading added on top of it instead of being refused.
